note: The answer correctly states the low-pH compensation problem and the ~50 percent error magnitude but omits the hydrogen-ion share of conductance the largest-source-of-error point the 25 °C equilibration check with its pass bar and the comment-field recording requirement. Unmet: cause: hydrogen ion has different transport properties and contributes a large share of conductance at low pH; at low pH the temperature correction can be the single largest source of error; describes the check of comparing in-situ reading against the same water equilibrated to 25 C; pass bar: within about 5 microsiemens per centimetre at or below 100 or about 3 percent above that; if an alternative low-pH compensation method is used the compensation factor has to be recorded in the comment field

The answer correctly attributes the erratic ORP to the bailed/decanted method and notes the DO/Eh/temperature restriction but omits the qualified-reporting allowance the in-situ-vs-recommended distinction the anoxic/reducing inert-gas restriction and the suction-lift pump warning. Unmet: Explains bailed/decanted samples cannot establish unqualified ambient Eh; acknowledges subsample section permits estimated explicitly qualified reporting; States ORP DO and temperature are required in situ where possible while pH conductivity and turbidity are only recommended; States that in anoxic or reducing groundwater subsample procedures must not be used at all unless handled under an inert gas; Warns a peristaltic or other suction-lift pump also must not be used for ORP or DO because negative pressure volatilises dissolved gases

The answer asserts the buffers are suitable for acidic water and misses every must-contain point (no 4/7/10 insufficiency no 1.68–10 accuracy range no bracketing requirement no ±10 °C buffer temperature no ±0.05 pH check). Unmet: States the usual 4/7/10 buffer set is not sufficient for acidic water and a pH 1.68 (or 2) buffer is needed; States the standard pH procedure is expected to be accurate over roughly pH 1.68 to 10; States the sample pH must fall inside the calibrated range so a 4/7/10 set does not bracket pH 3.2; States the calibration buffers must be within about 10 C of the sample temperature; States a check of the buffer nearest the sample pH should be within about 0.05 pH unit of its value at that temperature or the system is recalibrated

The answer gives the thermal-equilibrium timing and the 15-20/10-minute reading schedule but omits the airtight/oxygen-impermeable setup the ORP-vs-pH response asymmetry reporting Eh to the nearest 10 mV and logging the electrode system used. Unmet: states the measurement must be made in situ with a submersible instrument or through an airtight flowthrough system that eliminates aeration; states the tubing must be relatively impermeable to oxygen the fittings airtight and atmospheric oxygen purged from the tubing and flow channels before measuring; notes the ORP system responds more slowly than pH and asymmetrically taking longer in one direction than the other; States calculated Eh is reported to the nearest 10 mV.; states the temperature the electrode system used and the pH at the time of measurement must be recorded with the value

The answer only addresses temperature bias during transport (one point met) and never discusses the turbidity bench-measurement biases the rubric asks for (condensation cell orientation coloured water gas bubbles dirty cells equilibration effects) though it avoids the prohibited assertions. Unmet: Identifies condensation on the sample cell as a plausible source of bias when sample water is much colder than air; Names the other bench-measurement biases: cell orientation coloured water gas bubbles scratched or dirty sample cells; Explains the preference for in-situ or pumped dynamic measurement while requiring checks of both methods before deciding which reading is reliable; Notes that letting the sample equilibrate to ambient temperature reduces condensation but warming the sample can change particle associations in the water

The answer only partially addresses subsample qualifiers for temperature and refuses the flow-cell sampling question the rubric expected a real answer to missing all turbidity-specific points (qualifier prohibition storage limits on-site measurement). Unmet: Turbidity value measured on a subsample must not be reported without a value qualifier and a comment marking it as estimated and made on a subsample; Same restriction applies to temperature dissolved oxygen and Eh measured on a subsample; States plainly that a discrete turbidity sample must not be collected from the discharge passing through the flow-through chamber holding the other sensors; Gives the storage limits if the sample cannot be read on site: clean amber bottle out of sunlight chilled at or below 4 C held no longer than 24 hours; Notes turbidity is time sensitive and should be measured on site preferably in situ

The answer gives the ±0.2 °C accuracy requirement and the certified/traceable reference check but omits that verification is across the range of use rather than adjustment to a standard and never mentions a faulty thermistor causing wrong specific conductance. Unmet: Checking means verifying accuracy across range of use not adjusting to a standard like pH/conductivity; Faulty/drifting thermistor in conductivity cell produces wrong specific conductance

The answer gives the per-degree range the compensation formula the 0.019–0.020 factor and the 25 °C reference but omits the ±5 percent accuracy over 5–35 °C and pH 4–11. Unmet: States temperature compensation is typically accurate to ±5 percent for 5-35 °C and pH 4-11

The answer correctly gives barometric pressure (1 mm Hg checked barometer) temperature (0.1 °C) and conductivity for salinity correction but omits the one-point calibration goal the computed-from-signal/ionic-strength point the recalibration-if-droplets rule (and assumes an optical probe) and the manual salinity-correction timing/recalibration points. Unmet: Goal of one-point calibration: 100% oxygen-saturated environment with DO sensor and temperature sensor at same temperature; Reported concentration computed from sensor signal with temperature and ionic strength; sensor not measuring mg/L directly; Checks droplets on optical module and temperature sensor recalibrates if present; does not assume unidentified probe is optical; Manual salinity correction: USGS prefers applying after calibration and measurement; distinguishes automatic conductivity-based compensation; Manual salinity correction at calibration forces recalibration for each change in field salinity

The answer gives no per-parameter stabilization tolerances (temperature SC DO pH turbidity) and no 60-second thermal-equilibrium minimum and it violates a must-not by applying a single 'within about 10%' tolerance to all parameters. Unmet: gives the temperature criterion as about plus or minus 0.2 C; gives the specific conductance criterion as about plus or minus 5 microsiemens per centimetre at or below 100 and about plus or minus 3 percent above that; gives the dissolved oxygen criterion as about plus or minus 0.2 mg/L; gives the pH criterion as about plus or minus 0.1 unit; gives turbidity stabilization as ±0.5 TU or ±5 percent whichever is greater at or below 100 TU; above 100 TU uses ±10 percent; states the criterion is judged over five or more consecutive readings not a single pair; gives the minimum wait in surface water as at least 60 seconds for the sensors and sonde body to reach thermal equilibrium; states 60 seconds is a minimum and some instruments need longer per the manufacturer up to several minutes depending on the temperature step

The answer invents a discrepancy and declares one rule stricter ("The stricter 10 % rule is the immediate trigger") violating the must-not items and makes none of the required points. Unmet: States plainly that the two tables give the same stabilisation criteria and do not conflict; States the general field-measurement chapter itself points multiparameter users to the multiparameter chapter for criteria of the same kind; States the criteria are standard sensor stabilisation criteria and that actual sensor accuracy varies by model and manufacturer which is a separate matter; For persistent variability extends equilibration and records additional measurements then reports the median of the final five or more readings or selects a representative final reading with documented judgment

The answer correctly directs a ZoBell's-solution probe check and avoids the prohibited errors but it omits the temperature-dependent table value the ~430 mV at 25 C interpolation thermal-equilibration time the 5 mV reference-electrode-corrected pass window and the 90-day chilled stability. Unmet: States the expected ZoBell value is temperature dependent and must be read from the temperature table not taken as a single number; Gives the theoretical ZoBell Eh at 25 C as about 430 mV; States values for temperatures between table rows are interpolated; States the solution and sensors must be left to reach thermal equilibrium on the order of 15 to 30 minutes before the check is read; Gives the check pass window as calculated Eh after adding the appropriate reference-electrode potential to measured potential within 5 mV of the temperature-specific table value; States ZoBell's solution is reported stable for at least 90 days chilled at 4 C; does not invent a 90-day expiry

The answer correctly identifies low ionic strength and the circuit-completion problem and gives the KCl fix with the right mass and conductivity increase but omits the ionic-strength/liquid-junction explanation alternative electrode types the <0.01 pH figure and the warning against stirring the untreated subsample. Unmet: Names large ionic-strength difference between sample and buffers and enlarged liquid-junction potential; Recommends a different electrode type (fast-responding liquid-filled Ross combination or double-junction); States KCl addition changes measured pH by less than ~0.01 unit; Warns against stirring untreated low-conductance subsample while permitting gentle swirling to dissolve KCl

The answer is a bare refusal that makes none of the required points though it avoids the 'must not' violations. Unmet: states order matters and temperature first; gives specific conductance next before pH; gives remaining order pH DO ORP turbidity ion-selective/fluorescence with A6.2 DO-last exception; rationale: low to high ionic strength to avoid residual standard bias; conductivity before pH because pH buffers/filling solutions are high ionic strength contamination source; sensors rinsed three times with deionized water between standards; sonde calibrated or checked before each field use

The answer refuses the A6.8 example-form criteria the rubric asks for providing only the A6.4 final-buffer check and so missing the ±0.1 pH unit and ±0.3 pH unit below 75 µS/cm points and the required distinction. Unmet: Attributes ±0.1 pH unit to the A6.8 example field form's calibration criterion; Attributes ±0.3 pH unit below 75 µS/cm to that example form; Distinguishes the form's conductivity-dependent criteria from A6.4's final-buffer check (0.05 pH unit of certified value)

The answer correctly places the pH sensor downstream of the conductivity sensor but omits the cell-proximity/sunlight shielding and the design-dependent conductivity probe position. Unmet: states the flow cell should be kept as close to the source water as possible and shielded from direct sunlight; notes the specific-conductance probe position relative to the pH electrode depends on the flow-cell design

Only the pre-use calibration point is made; the exemption midday-drift qualification sonde deployment/recovery DO post-cal check details and QA-plan precedence are all missing and the answer violates a must-not by asserting the EPA routine is 'different from the USGS guidance' and that USGS requirements need not be applied a claim of disagreement between the two documents made without any supporting citation. Unmet: End-of-day check except when instrument is calibrated at each sampling location (stated exemption); Midday drift: recalibrate before later data unaffected and data preceding the check are qualified; Continuously deployed sonde calibrated before deployment and checked on recovery; DO post-calibration check in measurement mode recording DO temperature and barometric pressure against an oxygen-solubility chart; SOP's own drift criteria apply only when the project QA plan does not specify its own

The answer picks the EPA chart but supplies none of the required values (9.09 9.06 0.03 mg/L) no Benson and Krause note no ±0.2 mg/L tolerance comparison and does not frame the choice as using whichever protocol's table consistently. Unmet: gives the USGS table value at 20.0 C and 760 mmHg as about 9.09 mg/L; gives the EPA chart value at 20 C and 760 mmHg as about 9.06 mg/L; States the difference is 0.03 mg/L and assesses its significance against the applicable procedure; notes the USGS values are generated from the Benson and Krause equations; Compares the 0.03 mg/L difference with the USGS saturation-check tolerance of ±0.2 mg/L; advises using the table belonging to whichever protocol the work is being done under consistently rather than mixing them

The answer covers DO and pH temperature compensation but omits specific conductance and ORP as potentially affected gives no SC temperature-correction explanation and never notes the temperature sensor's separate location from the pH electrode. Unmet: Identifies pH dissolved oxygen specific conductance and ORP as potentially affected where their calculations or calibration rely on that temperature sensor; Explains for specific conductance that the reported value is a temperature-corrected number computed from the measured temperature; Explains for pH that the buffer values used to calibrate it depend on temperature; Notes that on a multiparameter instrument the temperature sensor typically sits in a different part of the instrument from the pH electrode

The answer is a bare refusal that withholds every requested table bound and comparison making none of the must-contain points though it avoids the must-not violations. Unmet: EPA chart temperature coverage runs to 45 C no value above; USGS solubility table stops at 40.0 C; USGS table extends down to 600 mmHg; EPA chart bottoms out around 690 mmHg; Explains different bounds; neither covers >40 C and <690 mmHg simultaneously; Only USGS chapter supplies salinity correction factors

The answer gives the traceable-thermometer check the ±0.2 °C tolerance and the annual cadence but it wrongly frames the temperature sensor as treated like a pH sensor (missing the verify-not-adjust point) and omits the calibration-solution/evaporation point. Unmet: States a temperature sensor is not adjusted to a standard like a pH/conductivity sensor; procedure is to verify accuracy across the range of use; States calibration solution must cover probe and temperature sensor; identifies evaporation of moisture as a DO air-calibration concern

The answer gives the multiplication method and cites table 6.2-4 but withholds the required factor 0.8235 declaring it unavailable which is a refusal of the figure the rubric asks for. Unmet: Gives 0.8235 as the factor for 20.0 °C at 50 000 µS/cm

The answer makes none of the required points about the 25 C reference and temperature compensation and it violates a must-not by telling the operator to use the pod's reported conductivity directly in the salinity correction table. Unmet: States the salinity correction table is indexed on specific conductance referenced to 25 C not raw conductivity at the water's own temperature; States a conductivity reading taken at any other temperature must be corrected to what it would read at 25 C before use; States most modern meters and sondes apply that temperature compensation automatically and report the 25 C value; Tells the operator to confirm whether the pod's conductivity output is already temperature-compensated; Notes A6.2 defines saline waters as specific conductance greater than 2 000 microsiemens per centimetre where the DO solubility correction varies with instrument type calibration method and salts

Four of five must-contain points are made correctly with citations but the answer never states that a small well-mixed stream under about 5 feet wide can be represented by a single centroid point. Unmet: Small well-mixed stream under about 5 feet wide can be represented by a single centroid point

The answer never mentions the 2 000 µS/cm operational threshold never asks for the upstream specific conductance and instead of giving 1.0000 at zero specific conductance it says the factor is merely 'very close to 1.0' and extends that to all the freshwater pods. Unmet: Explains the manual's operational saline-water correction applies above 2 000 µS/cm and asks for the upstream specific conductance before deciding; freshwater does not imply zero conductivity; Gives 1.0000 at zero specific conductance without extending that exact factor to all freshwater

The answer states the 0.3 mg/L variation exceeds the ±0.2 mg/L tolerance (point 2) but misses the consecutive-readings criterion the longer-equilibration/final-readings rule the surface/groundwater median distinction and the ORP note and it offers a mean as an alternative to the prescribed median violating a must-not. Unmet: Gives the USGS stabilisation criterion for optical DO as about ±0.2 mg/L across five or more consecutive readings; Allows longer equilibration and additional readings then either the median of the final five or more readings or a representative final reading selected using site knowledge and professional judgment with the decision documented; Gives the median rule as the final three or more readings in surface water or the final five or more in groundwater; Notes that ORP is not covered by that stabilisation table and is instead judged by the potential holding constant over the reading sequence

The answer states that diluting a strong standard to make weaker points is not recommended but omits the 4 000-unit formazin exception the suspension-matrix/non-linearity explanation and the recommendation to buy commercially prepared solutions at the needed values; no must-not item is violated. Unmet: gives 4 000-unit formazin as the one exception that may be diluted; explains that diluting changes the suspension matrix so the dilutions are no longer linear; recommends buying commercially prepared solutions at the values needed rather than preparing them by dilution

The answer gives the 60-second equilibration and the median-of-final-readings rule but never states that the per-vertical value is the median of readings observed within about 60 seconds after equilibration and it adds no forbidden instantaneous reading averaging or invented equilibration time. Unmet: States the value recorded at each vertical is the median of the values observed within about 60 seconds after the sensors have equilibrated

The answer rejects the bottle as expired and cites the one-day stability but it never mentions flocculation or the need to distinguish reversible settling from flocculation instead assuming any settled calibrant must be discarded. Unmet: States calibrants with flocculated suspensions must not be used; Requires checking reversible settling vs flocculation plus expiry/storage compliance and rejects flocculated/expired/compromised calibrant rather than assuming all settled calibrant must be discarded

Only the ±0.2 mg/L solubility-chart verification point is made; the wet sponge/towel setup no-touch rule 10–15 minute saturation time and on-site barometer restriction are missing (the answer gives 5–10 minutes instead). Unmet: 100 percent water-saturated air environment made with a wet sponge or wet paper towel in the bottom of the container; Neither the probe nor the temperature sensor may touch the wet sponge or towel; Roughly 10 to 15 minutes for the confined air to saturate while the instrument warms up; Barometric pressure must come from an on-site barometer not a weather service unless corrected for elevation

The answer refuses and claims the value is not in the excerpts withholding the 9.09 mg/L figure the rubric requires so no must-contain point is made. Unmet: Gives 9.09 mg/L for 20.0 °C at 760 mmHg; Attributes the value to the freshwater table in the USGS NFM chapter on dissolved oxygen (table 6.2-2); States the figure is for fresh water before any salinity correction

The answer gives a 0.2 mg/L zero-DO tolerance and manufacturer/luminophore troubleshooting instead of the rubric's 0.5 mg/L acceptance value the cleaning/membrane-and-electrolyte remedy and the accuracy-dependence note so none of the must-contain points are made. Unmet: States the instrument should read less than 0.5 mg/L in a 0.0 mg/L DO solution; States a reading above 0.5 mg/L or any negative reading calls for cleaning the probe and changing the membrane and electrolyte; Notes the 0.5 mg/L value assumes an instrument accuracy of about ±0.2 mg/L and may be adjusted to the project's or instrument's accuracy requirements

The answer refuses outright providing none of the required table values or the 2.14 mg/L decrease so it misses every must-contain point even though it invents nothing. Unmet: Gives 6.95 mg/L for 35.0 °C at 760 mmHg; States equilibrium saturation decreases by 2.14 mg/L about 2 mg/L; does not describe it as an absolute maximum excluding supersaturation; Takes both figures from the same USGS table rather than mixing sources

The answer gives the <3 µS/cm threshold and treats 6 µS/cm as above it but never explains that this is the meter's low-end zero-response check made with the dry cell in air or in deionized water. Unmet: Explains this is the meter's low-end zero-response check made with the dry cell in air or in deionized water

The answer correctly forbids DI water as a standard gives the nearest/bracketing standard with a 500 µS/cm example and separates the zero-response check from calibration but it omits the reason that standards above 200 µS/cm are recommended because lower ones are easily biased by dilution or contamination. Unmet: States calibration standards greater than 200 µS/cm are recommended because lower ones are easily biased by dilution or contamination

The answer gives the 60-second minimum and the thermal-equilibrium reason but never says some instruments need longer or that equilibration can run to several minutes depending on temperature difference. Unmet: States the 60 seconds is a floor and some instruments need longer per the manufacturer; Notes equilibration can run from 60 seconds to several minutes depending on the temperature difference

The answer correctly states the two-point minimum the ±2 °C extrema rule the ±4 °C mean rule and the 6/10 °C example but omits the note that this procedure requires at most five points. Unmet: Notes this range-verification procedure requires at most five points without generalizing to every certification procedure

The answer covers both acceptable methods the in situ annual route and the annual requirement but omits the required one-point pre-field-trip check against a certified sensor. Unmet: States a one-point check against a certified sensor is also required immediately before a field trip

The answer correctly gives the temperature DO pH and conductance stabilization tolerances but omits the >100 TU ±10 percent turbidity clause and states three to five readings rather than about five or more consecutive readings. Unmet: Turbidity ±0.5 TU or ±5 percent whichever greater at or below 100 TU; above 100 TU uses ±10 percent; Assesses stabilization over about five or more consecutive readings

The answer gives freshwater solubility values at 15 and 20 C and notes salinity and pressure effects but it uses 695 mmHg so it misses the 0.99 mg/L benchmark at 760 mmHg and never states the warming contribution cannot be established from these readings alone. Unmet: States freshwater equilibrium solubility at 760 mmHg falls by 0.99 mg/L from 15 C to 20 C as a conditional benchmark; States the actual warming contribution and the remaining site-specific drop cannot be established from these readings alone because pressure salinity and the initial saturation are not given
All three must-contain points are made (0.40 at nearest 0.05 64 at nearest 1 attributed to the USGS reporting-convention table) and no must-not item is violated.

The answer correctly gives both EPA 180.1 rounded values (0.40 and 65) but omits the point that USGS follows ASTM guidelines unless data were collected for drinking-water compliance under EPA 180.1 GLI Method 2 or ISO 7027. Unmet: Notes USGS follows ASTM unless drinking-water compliance under EPA 180.1 GLI Method 2 or ISO 7027

The answer asserts Eh and the probe's raw ORP output are interchangeable ("the numeric value your probe gives in mV is the Eh value") violating a must-not item and makes none of the required points about the standard hydrogen electrode or reference-electrode correction. Unmet: states that Eh is defined relative to the standard hydrogen electrode; states that Eh is an equilibrium potential developed at the boundary between a noble-metal electrode and the water and reflects the redox-active species in solution; states that the millivolts the probe reads are not Eh on their own because that raw reading is against the probe's own reference electrode; states that getting Eh means adding the reference electrode's own potential to the measured reading
All three must-contain points are stated with supporting quotes and no must-not item (invented wait time treating drift as settled/pass or discarding without recording drift) appears.

The answer is a bare refusal that withholds the explanation the rubric asks for making none of the three must-contain points. Unmet: states that Eh is not treated as a routine or direct field measurement; states that because of this it has no entry in the stabilisation criteria that the other field measurements have; names the properties that are treated as routine on-site measurements - water temperature dissolved oxygen specific conductance pH and turbidity

The answer correctly grounds the ZoBell's pre-field test but omits the temperature-corrected table comparison the 430 mV theoretical value at 25 °C and the stabilization/recording step while avoiding the prohibited inventions. Unmet: States the calculated Eh of ZoBell's must come within 5 mV of the table value for the solution's temperature; Gives 430 mV as the theoretical Eh of ZoBell's at 25 °C; States the reading must stabilize to within ±5 mV before the temperature and millivolt value are recorded

The answer attributes the label to calibration method/manufacturer instructions rather than the instrument's optical design and omits the wavelength bands detector arrangements and letter expansions the rubric requires. Unmet: label determined by instrument's optical design not preference; 400-680 nm broad-spectrum → NTU/NTRU/BU/AU/NTMU; 780-900 nm NIR → FNU/FNRU/FBU/FAU/FNMU; detector arrangement (90° nephelometry backscatter attenuation ratio multibeam) sets labels; expands NTU and FNU

The answer correctly distinguishes required (policy research/consensus) and recommended (several acceptable alternatives) but omits that the reason for the chosen recommended alternative must be documented. Unmet: when a recommended step is involved the reason for picking the option picked has to be written down

The answer states the departure must be independently quality assured and documented (not just logged) and extends the same record-and-review expectation to a recommended alternative without inventing a form/role or claiming required steps can never be departed from.

The answer correctly states no conversion is needed since mho and siemens are the same unit but omits the 1971 changeover the interchangeable terminology and the temperature-reference caveat. Unmet: Mhos were the normal reporting unit for older data changeover around 1971; Specific conductance specific electrical conductance and electrical conductivity are all used in the literature for this same measurement; Because electrical conductivity is not always referenced to a standard temperature the measurement or reference temperature must be reported and checked against older values

The answer states both immersion methods and the whole-sonde trade-off but never says the calibration is done in a separate vessel rather than the monitored water body. Unmet: States that either way the calibration is done in a separate vessel with the sensor sitting in the calibration standard not in the water body being monitored.

The answer states both configuration-dependent difficulties (isolation and bubble-free optical surface) but omits the practical rinsing/agitation steps and the steady-stand step and it adds unsupported reasons; no must-not item is violated. Unmet: Practical steps: rinse with deionized water then the standard work bubbles off by agitating the sonde or running the wiper; Sonde set steady — stood vertically on a flat surface or held in a stand

The answer correctly defines specific conductance as the conductance of 1 cm³ of solution at 25 °C and says the unit is normalized but it omits the resistance/siemens basis the cell-constant (spacing/area) relation and the distinction that µS/cm alone does not establish temperature compensation. Unmet: Raw conductance is the inverse of resistance measured in siemens; Conductivity equals conductance times the cell constant (spacing/area) a geometry-normalized property; Distinguishes conductivity from specific conductance at 25 °C; µS/cm alone does not establish temperature compensation

The answer gives the 5-percent hydrochloric acid soak and the manufacturer-guidance check but omits the detergent-first step and the warning against nitric acid/aqua regia; no must-not item is violated. Unmet: says to start with a detergent solution and only escalate to acid if that fails; warns that nitric acid aqua regia and anything else that etches platinum or gold must not be used because they will attack platinum and platinum-iridium electrodes

The answer gives the 2-hour maximum soak and the deionized-water rinse but never states that the manufacturer's recommendations govern the soak limit. Unmet: repeats or upholds that the manufacturer's recommendations govern so a shorter limit from the instrument maker wins

The answer names connections and weak batteries but omits the cable-break check and never distinguishes the erratic-reading checks from the dirty-sensor/expired-verification causes of inaccurate readings. Unmet: Points at a break somewhere in the cable; Distinguishes erratic-reading checks from dirty-sensor and expired-verification causes noting weak batteries can cause either

The answer warns that a cable replacement may require recertification and adds follow-up steps without inventing a recertification interval cost or provider and without presenting the swap as a no-follow-up field fix.

The answer is a bare refusal that withholds every fact the rubric asks for (24-hour hold 4 °C chilling amber bottle out of sunlight holding as a fallback) so no must-contain point is made. Unmet: states the sample must be held no longer than 24 hours; states it has to be chilled at or below 4 degrees Celsius; states it goes in a clean amber bottle and is kept out of sunlight; frames holding the sample as a fallback for when immediate measurement is not possible

The answer correctly says not to shake and to invert ~25 times but omits the 1-second inversion cycle the instruction to let bubbles clear before filling the cell and the guidance about avoiding reading straight from the bottle / pouring off immediately after mixing. Unmet: says to mix by turning the bottle end over end about 25 times roughly one turn per second; says to let the bubbles clear before filling the measurement cell; notes that reading straight from the bottle into the cell is best avoided and that if it cannot be avoided the sample is poured off immediately after mixing

The answer declines to set the alarm notes the pod threshold is unavailable and quotes the spectrophotometric verification trigger but omits the Rhodazine D 0.025–1.0 mg/L range point. Unmet: Notes Rhodazine D spectrophotometric method covers roughly 0.025 to 1.0 mg/L underscoring the figure is about verifying the instrument

The answer correctly says the pod threshold is unavailable and declines to judge 8.7 but it never gives the USGS chapter's 6.5 to 8.5 general river-water description nor frames it as a description rather than a limit. Unmet: States the USGS pH chapter describes river waters not affected by contamination as generally reading pH 6.5 to 8.5 attributed to that chapter; Makes clear this is a description of what such waters generally read not a criterion or limit the chapter sets

The answer declines to adopt 6.5–8.5 and distinguishes the documents' content from a pod alarm band but it refuses rather than giving the chapter's river-water and groundwater descriptions so most must-contain points are missed. Unmet: States 6.5–8.5 is the chapter's description of what uncontaminated river water generally reads not a limit it recommends configuring; States most groundwaters in the United States instead run 6.0 to 8.5 so a single freshwater figure does not necessarily fit both surface and groundwater sites; States this pod's configured threshold is unavailable here; no supplied result establishes whether one is configured

The answer declines to judge the reading and says the pod threshold is unavailable but it omits the relative/uncalibrated-index point and does not attribute the groundwater figures to the USGS chapter. Unmet: States the USGS chapter describes natural groundwater turbidity as generally less than 5 units up to 19 reported attributed to that chapter; States turbidity is a relative uncalibrated index here and is not judged against a numeric range

The answer declines to set a 19 NTU flagging threshold and notes the pod threshold is missing but it omits the contaminated-groundwater-higher figure the observed-not-recommended framing and the qualitative/relative nature of turbidity. Unmet: States the chapter reports natural groundwater turbidity up to 19 TU in some settings and that contaminated groundwater can run considerably higher attributed to that chapter; States the chapter's groundwater figures describe what has been observed not a value it recommends flagging on; Reiterates that turbidity is a relative qualitative indicator here not a value with a numeric pass/fail band

The answer correctly states the electrode must not go in the stock bottle that buffer is poured into a separate clean container and that the used portion is discarded but it omits the recommendation to decant into a labelled dedicated secondary bottle for field use. Unmet: Recommends decanting into a dedicated secondary bottle for field use labelled with its value lot number and expiration date

The answer is a bare refusal that withholds the requested guidance making none of the five must-contain points though it avoids the must-not items. Unmet: States that the decanted field bottles should be refreshed before every field trip; States that solution past its expiration date must not be used; States that the solutions must be protected from wide temperature swings and from extreme heat or freezing; States that solution which has been frozen or overheated can no longer be assumed valid and should be discarded; Notes that the lot number expiration date and the temperature at use are recorded in the instrument logbook

The answer states the pod threshold is unavailable and avoids declaring the reading in or out of range but it does not attribute the 1.0 mg/L hypoxic wording to the optical-sensor verification discussion or explain that the figure is a documentation trigger not an ecological limit. Unmet: Attributes the below-1.0 mg/L hypoxic-to-anoxic wording to the USGS optical-sensor verification discussion not a universal ecological definition; States that this 1.0 mg/L figure is the point at which the chapter requires an optical sensor's accuracy in that range to be independently documented before such data are reported not an ecological limit it sets for the pod

The answer correctly gives the ±0.2 mg/L or 2 percent verification check and properly declines the brackish-water part but omits the optical-surface check the conductivity-sensor requirement and both salinity-correction points. Unmet: For optical hardware checks optical module and temperature-sensor surfaces and repeats calibration if water droplets were present; States a calibrated conductivity sensor is needed in saline or brackish water; Prefers applying manual salinity correction after calibration and measurement; automatic compensation separate; Notes manual salinity correction during calibration forces recalibration for every field salinity change

The answer makes five of the six must-contain points (chamber wetting loose screw-on chamber 5-10 minute equilibration mm-of-mercury pressure reading 100-percent-saturation goal) but never states that barometric pressure must be measured at the calibration altitude rather than corrected from elsewhere and it avoids all the must-not items. Unmet: States that the barometric pressure must be measured at the altitude where the calibration is done rather than corrected from elsewhere

The answer correctly identifies TU as a generic turbidity-unit label and notes the method is unspecified but it never mentions light source/optical arrangement or the historical JTU/FTU labels and it avoids the forbidden equivalences. Unmet: states that because the instrument design is unknown the label does not tell you what light source or optical arrangement produced the number; warns that older data can also carry historical labels - Jackson turbidity units (JTU) or formazin turbidity units (FTU) - which are no longer in normal use

The answer states daily pre-use calibration the end-of-day drift check and that data may need qualification but omits the measurement-mode/standard-reading detail and the midday-recalibration qualification limit.
